trdCodingStandards: Match whatever the primary language above already uses as its ecosystem-standard formatter/linter (e.g. ESLint + Prettier for TypeScript, ruff/black for Python, gofmt for Go) — don't invent a custom convention.

Don't invent a house style — adopt whatever formatter/linter is already standard for the primary language above (ESLint + Prettier for TypeScript, ruff/black for Python, gofmt for Go) and enforce it in CI from day one.

Pick the boring, standard formatter/linter for the primary language above (ESLint + Prettier for TypeScript, ruff/black for Python, gofmt for Go) and never argue about style in review again — the tool decides, not the reviewer.
trdDependencyPolicy: Ask before adding a dependency not already implied by the stack above.
Treat the stack above as the full dependency list until proven otherwise — adding anything beyond it should be a deliberate decision, not a drive-by install.
Every dependency beyond what's listed above is a future maintenance cost — worth adding only when it clearly earns its place.
securitySecretsNote: All keys live in `.env`; `.env` is gitignored; never hardcode or log a secret value.
Every secret goes in `.env`, `.env` stays out of git, and no key is ever hardcoded or printed to a log — no exceptions.
Keep secrets in `.env` only — gitignored, never hardcoded, never logged, never pasted into a commit message either.
securityInputValidation: Validate every user-submitted field client-side for UX; if there's a backend (see Document 2), validate again server-side — client-side validation alone is never a security boundary.
Client-side validation is a UX nicety, not a security control — validate every user-submitted field again on the server (see Document 2) if this idea has one.
Assume every input is hostile until validated: client-side checks improve the experience, but only server-side validation (Document 2, if this idea has a backend) actually protects anything.
securityDependencyPolicy: Prefer actively-maintained packages; run `npm audit` (or your ecosystem's equivalent) before shipping.
Favor packages with recent commits and an active maintainer over ones that look abandoned — and run `npm audit` (or your ecosystem's equivalent) before every release.
An unmaintained dependency is a slow-motion security incident — check `npm audit` (or your ecosystem's equivalent) before shipping, and again periodically after.
testingDodIntro: A feature isn't done when it works once on your machine — it's done when it clears all five of these:
Use this checklist as the actual gate before calling any feature complete:
Nothing ships until every box below is checked, not just the ones that are convenient:
uiuxDesignSystemStarter:
- One accent color, everything else neutral gray — avoid decorating with more than one hue.
- A consistent spacing scale (e.g. 4px base unit).
- Dark and light mode from day one if your stack supports it easily.

- Pick exactly one accent color and let neutral grays do the rest of the work.
- Commit to a spacing scale early (a 4px base unit is a safe default) so nothing gets eyeballed later.
- Build dark mode in from the start if your stack makes it easy — retrofitting it later is always more painful.

- Restraint over decoration: one accent hue, neutral grays everywhere else.
- A fixed spacing scale (4px base unit works well) beats ad hoc pixel values every time.
- If dark/light mode is cheap in your stack, ship both from day one instead of bolting it on later.
uiuxMobileNotes: Stack everything to a single column below ~640px; keep the primary action reachable without scrolling.
Below roughly 640px, collapse to a single column and make sure the primary action never requires scrolling to reach.
Design mobile as the default, not an afterthought: single column under ~640px, primary action always in reach.
appFlowJourneyTemplate: Home → use **{feature}** → see the result → (optional) act on it → back to Home.
Start at Home, use **{feature}**, see what it produced, optionally act on it, then return to Home — that loop should never take more than a few clicks.
The whole point of Home is to get someone to **{feature}** as fast as possible — from there: see the result, act if needed, back to Home.
appFlowNavMap: Every screen should be reachable from a persistent nav, and every screen needs a way back out — no dead ends.
No dead ends: every screen needs both a way in (from persistent nav) and a way out.
If a screen isn't reachable from the main nav, or doesn't have an obvious way back, that's a bug — not a later polish item.
appFlowEdgeIntro: Design for these on purpose, before they show up as bug reports:
The edge cases that actually get reported in the wild:
Three paths that are easy to forget until a real user hits them:
agentRulesScopeBullet: Only change what the current task requires. Never refactor unrelated code without asking.
Stay inside the current task's scope — unrelated refactors need a separate conversation, not a drive-by fix.
Touch only what the task actually requires; if you spot something else worth fixing, mention it instead of fixing it silently.
agentRulesAskBeforeBullet: Ask before: adding a dependency, changing the data model, deleting files, or renaming anything project-wide.
Check first before: adding a new dependency, changing the data model, deleting a file, or a project-wide rename.
These need a yes first, not a heads-up after: new dependencies, data model changes, file deletions, project-wide renames.
agentRulesStuckBullet: If stuck after two failed attempts on the same problem: stop, explain what was tried, propose 2-3 options.
Two failed attempts at the same problem is the signal to stop and explain — not to try a third variation of the same approach.
After two failed tries: pause, summarize what didn't work, and lay out 2-3 real options instead of guessing again.
agentRulesReportBullet: After every task: report what changed, which files, and how to verify it.
Every completed task gets a short report: what changed, which files, how to check it worked.
Don't just say "done" — say what changed, where, and how to verify it before moving on.
